AM4F-01.note: 5(-2)-(-2)^2 = -10-4 = -14. All three distractors are sign-handling endpoints: 14 (whole expression negated), -6 ((-2)^2 read as -4), 6 (both). Options come as two +/- pairs, so nothing is free. Early-section easy.

AM4F-02.note: f(2)=9, g(9)=5. 9 is the intermediate and sits ON the ballot as a distractor; -2 = g(2); -7 = f(g(2)) with the composition reversed. Every wrong option is a named error. Note -7 + 5 = -2 among the options, but the key is inside that relation, not exposed by it.

AM4F-03.note: (x+9)/2 = 4 gives x = -1. 6.5 = h(4) (inverse ignored), 17 = 2(4)+9 (inverse mis-built), -5 = 4-9 (division dropped). Clean.

AM4F-04.note: 5d = 7-22 = -15, d = -3. The sequence is visibly decreasing, so 3 and 4 are eliminable on sign alone without solving - a 4-way item that is really 2-way. Of the survivors, -15 is the total change (the intermediate) and is a genuine error. 4 corresponds to no arithmetic I can name; it is the weak one.

AM4F-05.note: amplitude 4, midline 5, max = 9. 1 is the minimum (strong). 17 and 12 both come from reading the amplitude as 4*3 = 12, which is one error counted twice. Mild reachability worry: 1 and 9 straddle the stem-printed 5 by +/-4, so a test-wise student who spots the pair has the amplitude handed to them and picks the larger.

AM4F-06.note: SYMBOLIC. Option set alone narrows nothing: the four options are the complete 2x2 sign permutation, so no option is odd-man-out and the shift convention has to be known. Textbook easy.

AM4F-07.note: 2x+7=0. Options are the full sign-by-reciprocal permutation of 7/2, so the numerator/denominator confusion and the sign error are both on the ballot and nothing is eliminable by shape.

AM4F-08.note: RE-KEYED ITEM (the key is a power). a5 = a2*r^3, so r^3 = (5/3)/45 = 1/27. Reads naturally - arguably MORE natural than asking for r, since r^3 is what the ratio of terms directly produces and 'if r is the common ratio, what is r cubed' is ordinary ACT phrasing. Cost: it removes the cube-root step, so the item is easier than its unrepaired form. 1/3 = r, 3 and 27 = the two inversions. Good set.

AM4F-09.note: SYMBOLIC. Option set alone narrows nothing: base and exponent-denominator are crossed over {3, 8}, and the stem prints both numbers, so neither slot can be filled by elimination. The whole item is the modelling convention.

AM4F-10.note: RE-KEYED ITEM (the key is a total change). f(4)=48, f(1)=-3, change = 51. 'Total change in the value of f from x=1 to x=4' is standard wording and reads naturally - the least forced of the four re-keys. 48 = f(4) alone (strong, the classic endpoint-only error); 63 = 4^3-1^3 (the linear term dropped); 17 maps to no error I can construct and is weak. No option is the sum or difference of two others.

AM4F-11.note: f(1)=8 (lower branch), f(8)=60 (upper). 8 is the intermediate, on the ballot. 22 = 2(8)+6, wrong branch on the second call. 0 = 2(-3)+6, wrong branch on BOTH calls. Every distractor is a specific branch error.

AM4F-12.note: axis of symmetry x=3, partner of 1 is 2(3)-1 = 5. 3 is the vertex x (intermediate) and is a distractor. -1 and -5 are sign flips. 'exactly one number k, other than 1' is doing real work and the excluded value 1 is not on the ballot, which is correct here since 1 is named in the stem.

AM4F-13.note: sqrt(3x+4) = 7, 3x+4 = 49, x = 15. 7 is the intermediate radical value and is a distractor (strong). 0 comes from sqrt(3x+4)=2, i.e. the -5 dropped (strong). 5/3 implies sqrt = 3, which I cannot source to a natural slip - weak.

AM4F-14.note: SYMBOLIC (coordinate pair). h = -b/2a = -3, k = 9-18-1 = -10. Option set alone narrows nothing: x is +/-3 two-and-two and y is one of two values, a full 2x2 with no modal coordinate. 8 = (-3)^2 - 1, the 6x term dropped; 3 = sign error on the vertex formula. Clean.

AM4F-15.note: equal degrees, ratio of leading coefficients 6/2 = 3. 1/3 inverts it, 6/5 uses the wrong pair of coefficients, 0 assumes denominator dominates. Three named misconceptions.

AM4F-16.note: x+5 = 3^2 = 9, x = 4. 20 comes from 5^2 (base and part of the argument swapped) and 14 from 3^2+5 (subtraction direction reversed) - both fine. 1 requires x+5 = 6 = 2*3, a multiplication-for-exponentiation slip; thinner but real.

AM4F-17.note: f(-2) = -2, g(-2) = -12, difference = 10. -2 is the intermediate f(-2) and is a distractor; -14 is (f+g)(-2), the operation misread; -10 is the subtraction reversed. Tight set, and note the key is the only positive option - a guesser who notices that gets it free. That is the one blemish, though 'f minus g at a negative input' gives no reason to expect a positive answer, so I do not think it is exploitable.

AM4F-18.note: RE-KEYED ITEM (the key is a part of a total). After the first hour, 2h25m remains = 3 started hours at $3 = $9 (total would be $14). The re-key reads slightly forced - 'how many dollars of the total charge are for the time after the first hour' is clunkier than asking for the total - but the $5/$3 split makes the sub-question meaningful rather than arbitrary, so it lands. Partial reachability: 14 is on the ballot and 14 - 9 = 5, the stem-printed first-hour fee, so a student who computes the TOTAL can back into the key by subtracting a number the stem gives. That still requires the ceiling-function work, which is the actual skill. 6 = only 2 additional blocks counted (the classic error); 20 weaker.

AM4F-19.note: RE-KEYED ITEM (the key is a constant of variation). y = kx/z^2, 15 = 12k/4, k = 5. THIS IS THE FORCED ONE. The clause 'To find the value of y when x=6 and z=4, a student first finds the constant of variation' is pure scaffolding: x=6 and z=4 are never used by the question asked, and exist only so that 1.875 (the y the narrative promises and then does not ask for) can sit on the ballot. A real ACT stem would either ask for y or ask for k without the story. It is unambiguous and answerable, but the retrofit is visible - if any of the four gets rewritten, rewrite this one to just 'What is the constant of variation?' and drop the unused values. Distractors themselves are excellent: 1.875 = the abandoned final answer, 2.5 = z not squared, 45 = the relation inverted.

AM4F-20.note: min = 11 - b^2/4 = 2, b^2 = 36, b = -6 given the sign constraint. The disambiguating clause is doing real work and PASSES the inverse check: +6, the option the clause exists to exclude, is on the ballot. +/-3 come from stopping at b/2 = 3. Solid, if routine.

AM4F-21.note: h(x) = 2(x/4+3)-1 = x/2+5; x/2+5 = 9 gives x = 8 (verified h(8)=9). 12.5 = solving g(f(x))=9, the composition order reversed - the best distractor here. 9.5 = h(9), inverse ignored. 5 = f^-1(9), the intermediate. Three real errors, all reachable by a student who does most of the work.

AM4F-22.note: at t=12, A = 12,590.85 vs B = 12,600 (A still behind by 9); at t=13, A = 13,598 vs B = 12,900. Answer 13. Genuinely hard and the hardest item here: the crossing is decided by a 0.07% margin, so anyone who rounds 1.08^12 to two figures picks 12. That makes 12 a superb distractor - but it also means the item punishes rounding rather than reasoning, so it is knife-edge by construction. I would keep it; just be aware it is fiddly-hard, not conceptually hard. 41 and 8 correspond to nothing and are weak.

AM4F-23.note: SYMBOLIC (interval). Need 1/(x-6) - 2 >= 0 with x != 6: only x > 6 works, and 1 >= 2(x-6) gives x <= 6.5; at x = 6.5 the radicand is exactly 0, so 6.5 is included. THIS IS THE ONE SYMBOLIC ITEM WHERE THE OPTION SET DOES REAL WORK: all four options share the endpoints 6 and 6.5, so the hard half of the problem - discovering that 6.5 is the boundary at all - is handed over, and the student is left deciding two inclusivities, which sqrt (>= 0, include) and division (exclude) settle almost reflexively. The answer is still unique and the reasoning genuine, so not exclusive:false, but rate this medium-with-options rather than the hard it would be in free response. Distractors are the three inclusivity permutations, each a real error.

AM4F-24.note: 3x-9 = +/-15 gives x = 8 or -2; greatest is 8. The 'greatest' qualifier is load-bearing and PASSES the inverse check: -2, the root it exists to exclude, is on the ballot. 24 = 15+9 with the division dropped; 2 = sign error inside the bars.

AM4F-25.note: 12/(1-r) = 20, 1-r = 3/5, r = 2/5. 3/5 is the intermediate and is a distractor. -2/5 and -2/3 cover the sign slip and solving 12/(1+r). Clean; only caution is that |r| < 1 is satisfied by all four, so no free elimination.

AM4F-26.note: SYMBOLIC (coordinate pair). Cancels to y = x+2 with a hole at x = 5, so (5, 7). HERE THE OPTION SET DOES NARROW IT. The coordinate 7 appears in two options and 3 and 0 once each, so the modal y is 7; x = 5 is the value the stem literally prints in the denominator. A student who does no algebra beyond 'the hole is where the denominator vanishes' and then takes the repeated y-value lands on the key. The factoring step - the actual content - can be skipped. Worth re-dealing: give the two x = -2 options distinct y-values that do not repeat 7. Distractors: (-2, 0) is the x-intercept of the simplified line (good), (-2, 7) swaps the root in (fair), (5, 3) I cannot source (weak).

AM4F-27.note: 5, 7, 11, 19. 11 = a(3), the off-by-one intermediate, and 37 = a(5), the off-by-one the other way - both strong and they bracket the key, which is the right shape for a recursion item. -2 corresponds to no plausible slip and is weak. Straightforward once the recursion is read correctly.

AM4F-28.note: 240 * (1/2)^(15/6) = 42.43, so 42. 182 = 240 * (1/2)^(6/15), the exponent inverted - excellent. 60 = 240/4, only the two WHOLE half-lives counted, which is the error the 'to the nearest gram' and the non-integer 15/6 are designed to catch. 96 thinner. The rounding instruction is doing real work rather than decorating.
